Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Pattern is the paper blueprint every garment starts from. House is the older word for a small fashion practice. The brand sits at the technical origin of clothing, not the styled result.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern fashion brands are competing on transparency and design language. The customer wants to know who made the clothes and how. Brands that look like product companies, with a clear material story, are winning the design-literate audience.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Studio Nicholson (studionicholson.com) holds the modern restrained womenswear position. Aeron (aeron.co) does it from Eastern Europe with a sharper hand. The Row (therow.com) is the tier above. Cos (cosstores.com) sits in the accessible middle. We sit closest to Studio Nicholson with a more visible production process.
Modern.positioningStatement: Modern clothing built from the pattern up, with every step shown.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Buys six pieces a year. Reads about the maker. Pays for the fabric. Wears a piece three times a week for five years. Owns one good coat.

dos: Name the fabric and the mill
Show the pattern, the seamstress, the run
Speak to the customer who already knows what's good
donts: Run a runway show without buyers in the room

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark. PATTERN HOUSE in a precise modern grotesk, all caps, two words stacked on hangtags and on one line on the website. A small geometric mark, two parallel pattern-piece outlines, used as the hangtag stamp and the social profile.

colorPalette.name: Pattern Paper
colorPalette.meaning: Manila tag, tracing paper, the studio table.

colorPalette.name: Marker Ink
colorPalette.meaning: The fabric pen on the studio table.

colorPalette.name: Stitch Red
colorPalette.meaning: Stitch thread on muslin. The single accent.
colorPalette.usage: Hangtag accent, web headlines, sale signage

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for size charts and material specs
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the technical garment data (gauge, gsm, composition). The regular carries the brand.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No seasonal collections. No mannequin photography. No 'investment piece' copy. No collaborations with celebrity stylists.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A studio store open three days a week. A printed catalogue twice a year. Each garment ships with a hangtag listing the fabric, the mill, the seamstress, and the make-time. The website loads the production process before the lookbook.

Modern.brandNameRationale: Single word. Offcut is the industry term for the fabric scraps left over after a pattern is cut. The brand sits on the part of fashion that usually gets thrown away. Modern, slightly self-aware, immediately legible to anyone who has been near a sewing room.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern fashion has been moving toward circularity and material honesty. Customers are tired of the over-production cycle. The opening is for a brand that puts material reuse in the brand position, not as a marketing claim but as the actual product.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Christy Dawn (christydawn.com) holds the dead-stock peer position. Reformation (thereformation.com) sits in the sustainable scale tier. Stella McCartney (stellamccartney.com) does the institutional sustainability middle. We sit smaller and more honest than any of them.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern fashion brand made from what other brands cut and threw away.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Reads about fashion sustainability. Pays a premium for clothing made from reused materials. Owns fewer pieces and wears them longer.

dos: Name the source fabric and where it came from
Show the original off-cut next to the finished garment
Skip the lifestyle copy
donts: Use the word sustainable as a marketing word

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. OFFCUT in a precise grotesk, all caps. A small geometric mark, two thin angled lines suggesting fabric scissors, used as the hangtag stamp and the favicon.

typography.secondary: GT America Mono for size charts and material specs
typography.rationale: One family. Mono carries the fabric data.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No seasonal collections. No virgin materials. No 'conscious' marketing campaigns. No celebrity-stylist collaborations.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A studio store open three days a week. A printed catalogue twice a year. Each garment ships with a hangtag listing the source fabric and the original brand.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Burchill is an English surname with a tailoring register. Easy to associate with Savile Row even if the house is new. & Co. closes it like a small heritage firm. The whole name sounds like it has been on a brass plaque for a century.
Luxury.story: Burchill & Co. began with a master tailor who had spent decades inside larger English houses and wanted to do fewer commissions, more carefully. The house takes a limited number of clients each year. Some have been with the house since it opened.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end fashion has been chasing brand at the expense of craft. There's a smaller market for old tailoring done well. Bespoke garments, made by hand, sold by relationship. The customer is paying for the house, the tailor, and the next fitting.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Anderson & Sheppard (anderson-sheppard.co.uk) is the institutional reference. Henry Poole (henrypoole.com) holds the Savile Row tradition. Huntsman (huntsmansavilerow.com) is the closest peer. We belong in their company.
Luxury.positioningStatement: An English tailoring house for clients who measure their wardrobes in decades.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Owns at least one piece of bespoke clothing already. Buys for milestones (birthdays, anniversaries, ascensions). Expects the garment to last a lifetime.

dos: Address the client by surname
Speak in the language of cloth and cut
Send a paper card for every fitting

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the house's hallmark, stamped on the inside lining of every garment, the cover of the order book, and the brass plaque outside the showroom.

colorPalette.name: House Green
colorPalette.meaning: Tailoring chalk on wool. Old fitting room walls.

colorPalette.name: Heritage Brass
colorPalette.meaning: Aged metal. The hardware on the showroom door.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and order book
typography.secondary: Söhne for the showroom's few digital surfaces
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles correspondence. Both restrained.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No ready-to-wear. No e-commerce. No collaborations. No celebrity dressing. No press placements paid or unpaid.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two distinctive surnames joined by an ampersand. Stoneham is a heritage English-American name; Vail is short, sharp, and slightly American. The uneven rhythm makes the pair feel like a real partnership rather than a typed-up heritage name.
Luxury.story: Stoneham & Vail began with two principals who had spent decades inside larger tailoring houses and wanted to take fewer clients, more carefully. The house takes a limited number of clients each year. Some clients have been with the house since the 1960s.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end tailoring has been chasing brand at the expense of craft. There's a smaller market for old tailoring done well. Bespoke garments, made by hand, sold by relationship.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Anderson & Sheppard (anderson-sheppard.co.uk) is the institutional reference. Henry Poole (henrypoole.com) holds the Savile Row tradition. Huntsman (huntsmansavilerow.com) is the closest peer. We belong in their company on the smaller, more discreet side.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small tailoring house for clients who measure their wardrobes in decades.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy, often inherited. Owns at least one piece of bespoke clothing. Buys for milestones. Expects the garment to last a lifetime.

dos: Address the client by surname
Speak in the language of cloth and cut
Send a paper card for every fitting

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the house's hallmark, stamped on the inside lining of every garment, the order book, and the brass plaque outside the showroom.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and order book
typography.secondary: Söhne for the few digital surfaces
typography.rationale: A high contrast classical serif sets the heritage tone.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No ready-to-wear. No e-commerce. No collaborations. No celebrity dressing.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Three words, one process. Cut & Sew is the literal description of how clothing gets made before the brand layer is applied. The name puts the work in the brand position. Honest. Old. Unpretentious.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most fashion brands lead with the look. We lead with the make. The customer wants clothing that was actually made by someone, not assembled. The category needs a brand that says so plainly.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Many small fashion brands operate in this aesthetic space. None have claimed the language as bluntly. The closest spirit is Margiela's blank-tab tradition, applied to a smaller, quieter line.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Clothing cut and sewn, made to last, sold without marketing.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who already buy fewer, better clothes. They don't need a brand world. They want to know who made the garment and how long it will hold up.

dos: Show the seam
Name the fabric
List the make time
donts: Photograph clothes on white models against white walls

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. CUT & SEW in a single weight grotesk, all caps, wide spacing, three short marks on a line. No icon. Each garment has a small woven label inside that carries the wordmark, the size, and the make time. That is the whole identity system.

typography.rationale: One face. The garment label and the website are the same wordmark, the same size hierarchy, the same nothing.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No seasonal drops. No collaborations. No newsletter sign-up gates. No celebrity wears. No archive sales.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: One word. The verb every fashion brand dances around. We picked the action and stopped there. No suffix, no city, no founder name. The label inside the shirt says WEAR. That is the whole instruction.
Minimal.manifesto: Most fashion brands write a paragraph where one word would do. They name a feeling, a place, a season, a mood. We make clothes you wear. The brand is the thing in your hand. Hold it up. If you would wear it, take it home. That is the brief.
Minimal.industrySummary: Quiet luxury is a crowded shelf now. The opening underneath it is louder and simpler: a brand that strips the language back further than COS or Uniqlo and lets the garment do the talking. The customer is tired of being sold to.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: COS (cos.com) is the reference for plain modern dressing. Uniqlo (uniqlo.com) holds the everyday slot. Asket (asket.com) owns the permanent collection idea. We sit a step further out than Asket, with even less language around the product.
Minimal.positioning: WEAR is a clothing brand for people who are done reading about clothes. The collection is small, the names are descriptive, and the only marketing is the garment itself. Buy the shirt. Wear the shirt.
Minimal.targetAudience: Adults 28 to 50 who have bought their last trend piece. They know their measurements, they re-buy what works, and they read the label more than the campaign. Most of them got here after a few expensive mistakes.
Minimal.personality: Plainspoken. Patient. Unbothered by what is happening on the other side of the shop window. Says one thing and lets it sit.
Minimal.voiceAndTone: Captions are the product. 'White shirt. Cotton. Made in Portugal.' That is the post. No setup, no story, no hashtag.

messagingPillars.title: The garment is the message
messagingPillars.body: We do not write around the product. We label it. Shirt. Trousers. Coat. The photograph shows it on a person. The page says what it is made of and where.

messagingPillars.title: Small collection, kept
messagingPillars.body: Twelve pieces, always available. We add one a season and only if it earns its space. Nothing is retired to make room for novelty.

messagingPillars.title: No campaign
messagingPillars.body: We do not run seasonal campaigns. We re-shoot the same twelve pieces every year on different people. That is the marketing.

Minimal.logoDirection: Wordmark only. WEAR set in a plain grotesque, slightly wide, all caps. Printed small on a woven label inside the collar. Nothing on the outside of the garment.
Minimal.colorPalette: Paper white #FAFAFA for the site. Ink #0E0E0E for type. The clothes themselves are the color story.
Minimal.typography: One typeface throughout. A neutral grotesque, regular weight only. Body 16px, headlines 28px. No italics, no bold.

Corporate.tagline: Apparel manufacturing and distribution at scale.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Heritage signals longevity and quality. Apparel is the buyer-side word for the category. Partners closes it as a B2B service relationship. The whole name reads like a real, established apparel firm already on a Fortune 500 sourcing panel.
Corporate.industrySummary: Apparel manufacturing and licensing is a multi-billion dollar B2B category dominated by older players. The buyers are department stores, brand licensees, and retailers. The vendors compete on production reliability, quality control, and operational scale.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Li & Fung (lifung.com) is the global giant. PVH Corp (pvh.com) holds the brand-house side. Hanesbrands (hanes.com) sits in the manufacturing tier. G-III Apparel Group (g-iii.com) holds the licensing-heavy peer position. We sit smaller, more design-led, and more flexible.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Apparel manufacturing and licensing for brands at scale.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Retailers and brand licensees want production partners with operational discipline and a design-led understanding of the category. We sit in the middle, more design-aware than the giants, more reliable than the boutiques.

targetAudience.primary: Heads of Sourcing, VPs of Production, and Licensing Directors at retail chains, brand holding companies, and apparel licensees. They sign multi-season production contracts.
motivations: Quality control that survives buyer review

dos: Lead with production capacity
Show quality control metrics
Speak to the buyer, not the consumer

messagingPillars.name: Production at scale
messagingPillars.description: From design through delivery, single partner across multiple production cycles.

messagingPillars.name: Quality controls built in
messagingPillars.description: Audit-grade quality assurance across every production run, with reporting back to the buyer.

messagingPillars.name: One partner across categories
messagingPillars.description: Cut and sew, knit, accessories, and licensing under one contract.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single thread-and-needle silhouette reduced to two crossing strokes. Reads cleanly on a sourcing deck, a sample tag, and a B2B trade show banner.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and B2B materials
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed RFPs and licensing contracts
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles printed B2B documentation and licensing contracts.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No consumer brand of our own. No D2C ecommerce. No celebrity partnerships. No retail stores. The firm sells through B2B sourcing, not Instagram.

Corporate.tagline: Garment manufacturing, sourcing, and distribution for North American brands.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Burlow is a surname pulled from a 1940s pattern-maker who never got famous. Apparel Group is what the entity is. Together it sounds like a holding company that has been around longer than it has, which is the point. The name signals trade buyer, not consumer.
Corporate.manifesto: We do not run a fashion brand. We run the factory floor, the sourcing trips, the QA lines, and the freight schedules that brands depend on. Our customer is the merchandiser, the production lead, the founder who needs a partner that picks up the phone in February and is still on the line in November.
Corporate.industrySummary: Apparel sourcing is fragmented and increasingly nearshore. Buyers want shorter lead times, smaller MOQs, and a partner who can absorb the operational load. The vendors who win are the ones who feel less like factories and more like extensions of the brand team.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Li & Fung (lifung.com) remains the global reference. Suuchi (suuchi.com) has built the tech-forward story. Indigenous Designs (indigenousdesigns.com) holds the ethical mid-market. We sit in the practical middle: serious operations, North American footprint, no PR theater.
Corporate.positioning: Burlow Apparel Group is a manufacturing and distribution partner for emerging and mid-market apparel brands. We handle sourcing, production, QA, and warehousing so brand teams can focus on design and customer.
Corporate.targetAudience: Founders and production leads at apparel brands doing $2M to $50M in annual revenue. They have outgrown their first factory and need a partner who can scale with them without losing the craft conversation.
Corporate.personality: Senior. Operational. Speaks in production calendars and landed cost. Comfortable in the back of house. Does not need to be in the campaign.
Corporate.voiceAndTone: Direct, specific, and unembellished. We talk about CMT pricing, fabric mills, and shipping windows. Decks have numbers, not adjectives.

messagingPillars.title: Sourcing
messagingPillars.body: Vetted mill and trim relationships across Portugal, Peru, and the U.S. Southeast. Fabric library and sample turnaround inside 14 days. Tariff and origin documentation handled in-house.

messagingPillars.title: Production
messagingPillars.body: MOQs from 250 units. In-line QA on every run. Production planning shared with brand teams in a working document, not a black box.

messagingPillars.title: Distribution
messagingPillars.body: 3PL partners in Atlanta and Reno. Direct-to-retail and direct-to-consumer fulfillment under one purchase order. Returns processing and refurb included.

Corporate.logoDirection: Burlow set in a serif with a small caps Apparel Group beneath it on a single rule. A trade-buyer mark, not a consumer mark. Used on invoices, contracts, and trade-show booths.
Corporate.colorPalette: Charcoal #2A2A2A primary, oat #E8E1D2 secondary, factory red #B23A2D as a single accent. Restrained, industrial, slightly American.
Corporate.typography: A traditional serif for the wordmark, a clean grotesque for documents and tables. Numbers tabular, hierarchy disciplined.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Off Season is the fashion-industry term for inventory and timing outside the main cycle. We named the brand after the moment most brands avoid. The name says we don't follow the calendar. Loud, plain, slightly cheeky.
Creative.manifesto: Most fashion brands chase the season. New season, new drop, new sale on the old season. We made Off Season because the rhythm of fashion is exhausting and the clothes are mostly the same. Buy when you want. Wear what holds up. The season is a marketing exercise.
Creative.industrySummary: Fashion has been organized around four seasons for a hundred years. The customer is over it. There's room for a brand that ignores the calendar, releases when the work is done, and treats every garment as the off-season version of itself.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Online Ceramics (onlineceramics.com) does the merch-as-brand thing well. Aimé Leon Dore (aimeleondore.com) has the cultural side. Story Mfg (storymfg.com) holds the slow-craft Creative position. We are sharper and louder than Story Mfg, less merch-y than the others.
Creative.positioningStatement: A fashion brand that releases when the work is done, not when the season says.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 40. Buys clothes from a small number of brands. Hates being told there's a sale ending. Wears the brand without thinking about it.

dos: Make jokes about the fashion calendar
Tell the customer when not to buy
Photograph the clothes on people who actually wear them
donts: Photograph the clothes against marble or white

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy display serif with the F in OFF stylized as a strike-through, suggesting that this is the version that doesn't follow the rules. Standalone strikethrough-F icon for hangtags, stickers, and social profiles.

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and hangtag info
typography.rationale: Migra has personality and warmth. Neue Montreal keeps the practical bits readable. The pair feels designed and a little weird.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not a seasonal brand. Not a sale brand. Not a luxury brand pretending to be quiet. Not too cool to make a joke about itself.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Hangtags with the worst quote from the customer review on them. Stickers in every order. A merch line of two tees and one hoodie, always available. A pop-up shop once a year in a city the brand doesn't ship to.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words that read like a note your sharper friend would write you. DRESS BETTER is bossy on purpose. The brand assumes the customer already knows they could be doing better and just needed someone to say it. The name is the entire pitch.
Creative.manifesto: We started because everyone we know dresses worse than they could. Not for lack of taste, for lack of nerve. They own one good shirt and wear the bad one. They have a great coat at the back of the closet because they are saving it. We made DRESS BETTER to take the saving-it out. Wear the coat. Wear the shirt. The occasion is Tuesday.
Creative.industrySummary: Fashion content is full of inspiration and empty of instruction. Customers do not need another mood board. They need a brand that points at one piece and says wear this, today, with what you already own. There is a real opening for a brand built around the imperative.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Permanent Style (permanentstyle.com) holds the menswear instructional position with a heavier tone. Blackbird Spyplane (blackbirdspyplane.com) owns the recommendation voice. Throwing Fits (the podcast) does the loud opinion. We sit between the instructional and the loud, with our own clothes attached.
Creative.positioning: DRESS BETTER is a clothing brand that talks like a friend with stronger opinions than you. We sell a small collection of upgrade pieces and a weekly note telling you which one to put on.
Creative.targetAudience: Adults 25 to 45 who have an okay wardrobe and a quiet suspicion they could do better. They have the budget, they do not have the time to figure it out, and they want someone to just tell them.
Creative.personality: Bossy in a kind way. Confident. A little impatient. The friend who reorganizes your closet uninvited and is mostly right about it.
Creative.voiceAndTone: Instructions, not invitations. 'Wear this shirt with the trousers you wore yesterday.' 'Roll the sleeves once, not twice.' 'Throw out the brown belt.' Short. Specific. Read like a text.

messagingPillars.title: The note
messagingPillars.body: A weekly email called 'Wear this on Wednesday.' One piece, one outfit, one instruction. No story, no scroll. People forward it. That is the only growth channel.

messagingPillars.title: The upgrade
messagingPillars.body: Twelve pieces a year. Each one replaces something most people already own a worse version of. We say what it replaces on the product page.

messagingPillars.title: The clinic
messagingPillars.body: Once a month we open the inbox and answer outfit questions with one-line replies. Screenshots get posted with the customer's permission. The clinic is the brand.

Creative.logoDirection: DRESS BETTER set in a chunky display sans, all caps, slightly condensed, almost looking like a road sign. Used at large scale on packaging and email headers. The mark is a command.
Creative.colorPalette: Marker red #E11A1A as the headline color. Notebook cream #F4EFE3 as the page. Ink #181818 for type. Reads like a handwritten note someone slapped on the fridge.
Creative.typography: One display sans for the instructions. One quiet serif for the product names. Body type left-aligned and short. Never centered.
